records.content: Azernews.Az Friday, August 14, 2026 Login Latest NATION WORLD BUSINESS OIL & GAS ARMENIAN-AZERBAIJANI RELATIONS EDITORIAL ANALYSIS LIFESTYLE EVENTS HEALTHCARE CULTURE SPORTS OUR WRITERS H5N1 spreads across Australia as authorities race to protect vulnerable birds 11 August 2026 11:08 (UTC+04:00) AzerNEWS Staff Read more Australia is preparing to vaccinate vulnerable native bird species kept in captivity as the highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu continues to spread across the country, local media reported on Tuesday. The country has recorded more than 230 confirmed cases of the virus, while authorities last week reported Australia’s first mass wildlife deaths associated with H5N1, according to ABC News. Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the vaccination programme would be rolled out across Australia’s states and territories in the coming days. She said authorities could not prevent H5N1 from spreading among wild birds but could take steps to safeguard species considered most vulnerable to the disease. Under the programme, officials will decide which species should receive the vaccine based on their susceptibility to the virus and the potential consequences for conservation efforts. Environment Minister Murray Watt said vaccinating wild birds on a large scale would not be practical because the vaccine requires two doses. However, targeted vaccination of wild birds could be considered where it is logistically possible. The Australian government has initially allocated A$2 million ($1.3 million) for vaccines. Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson said vaccination alone would not be sufficient to control the outbreak, emphasising that strong biosecurity measures would continue to play a key role in limiting the virus’s spread. H5N1 cases have now been confirmed across most of Australia, with Tasmania, the Northern Territory and the Australian Capital Territory the only jurisdictions yet to report infections. Despite the spread among wild birds, authorities have so far found no evidence of H5N1 in poultry or the wider agricultural sector. records.content: Bird baths posed similar risks because they draw birds into close contact and can become contaminated if not cleaned regularly, he said. The warning comes as New Zealand continues to monitor the arrival of H5N1 avian influenza following the country’s first two confirmed cases . The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) says there have been no further detections since July 17 and there is no evidence of mass mortality in wildlife or any detection in poultry. Surveillance has been stepped up. Across the Tasman, the situation has escalated in recent weeks, with Australian authorities confirming more than 50 H5N1 detections in wild seabirds across five states, including local transmission among greater crested terns in South Australia and a mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks. Last week, the virus spread beyond coastal species, with Australia’s first land-based bird death confirmed in a magpie in southwest Victoria – marking a significant shift inland in the outbreak’s reach. The risk of H5N1 avian bird flu spreading is greater anywhere birds gather in large numbers. Photo / Sarah Curtis Experts say the disease spreads more rapidly among birds that breed or congregate in dense numbers because the virus spreads rapidly through close contact and contaminated environments. McLean noted that bird feeders were already a vector for disease and need to be cleaned regularly, as bird faeces in and around the food could cause and spread Salmonella infections, avian pox and intestinal parasites. “Large concentrations of birds around garden feeders also cause aggression and this can skew the local diversity of birds in favour of already abundant species.” He said bird enthusiasts could better assist local birds by planting native plants and trees, restoring the environment and controlling pests. “Planting a layered mix of ground covers, shrubs and trees in your garden can provide insects, nectar, fruit, seeds, nesting sites and shelter for many native bird species,” McLean said. The arrival of H5N1 has also prompted concern among pet owners. Wairarapa veterinarian Dr Louisa Broughton told RNZ that while infections in cats are considered rare, H5N1 can have a high mortality rate when it does occur. She said owners concerned about the risk could reduce exposure by keeping cats away from sick or dead birds. Biosecurity Minister Andrew Hoggard has also advised dog owners not to allow pets to eat dead birds found on beaches or elsewhere. Overseas, H5N1 has infected a range of mammals , including cats and dogs, prompting authorities to issue similar warnings. Bird expert Ian McLean says instead of using feeding stations, bird lovers can encourage birds into their gardens by planting species that provide insects, nectar, fruit, seeds, nesting sites and shelter. Photo / Sarah Curtis MPI chief veterinary officer Dr Mary van Andel said the risk to pets in New Zealand remains “very low”, noting that cases overseas have generally occurred in places where the virus is circulating widely in wild birds or other animals. “In rare instances, dogs can become infected, but those that do rarely become seriously unwell,” van Andel said. “They can pick up the virus by mouthing infected birds, so all dogs should be kept away from sick or dead birds and other wildlife.” While it’s similarly rare, cats can also become sick through consuming contaminated animal products such as raw milk. The ministry says pet owners should prevent wild birds from accessing pet food and water; keep dogs on a leash near wild birds, keep cats indoors or discourage hunting behaviour; and ensure pets don’t touch or eat sick or dead animals. Sarah Curtis is a news reporter for the Northern Advocate , focusing on a wide range of issues. She has nearly 20 years’ experience in journalism, most of which she spent reporting on the courts in Gisborne and the East Coast

records.content: World Australia to vaccinate birds against H5 avian influenza As of yesterday, authorities have reported there are 231 confirmed or presumed positive detections of H5 bird flu in Australia. — Leanne Buchan/Leanne Buchan Photography handout pic via AFPF Tuesday, 11 Aug 2026 4:17 PM MYT SYDNEY, Aug 11 — Australian authorities said today they would vaccinate bird species deemed to be especially vulnerable to the highly contagious H5 bird flu virus. The country was for years the only continental landmass free of the H5 strain, which has caused severe disease and death in poultry and wild birds worldwide. The first Australian case was discovered in a migratory sea bird in June and last week the government reported its first mass mortality event in wildlife. As part of efforts to protect birds, officials said they would roll out targeted vaccinations for both captive and wild species. “It is difficult to vaccinate birds in the wild — it does take two vaccination doses to vaccinate birds,” environment minister Murray Watt said. “It is difficult to catch wild birds once, let alone twice,” he said. “Where it is possible to vaccinate wild birds, we will do so, but the priority is to vaccinate birds that are in captivity.” Agriculture minister Julie Collins said Australia should expect to see more mass bird deaths. “This will continue to spread across the country,” she said. The wild birds most affected by the H5 strain include waterfowl, shorebirds, seabirds and birds of prey. As of yesterday, authorities have reported there are 231 confirmed or presumed positive detections of H5 bird flu in Australia. There have been no cases detected in poultry or in the country’s agriculture production. Almost half of Australia’s wild bird species, and 83 per cent of its mammals, are found nowhere else. The H5 bird flu strain killed more than 13,000 elephant seal pups after infecting a breeding colony on the remote Heard and McDonald Islands, Australian scientists said in June. — AFP You May Also Like

records.content: Asia - Pacific Australia’s New South Wales confirms bird flu cases in native birds Latest cases involve greater crested terns found dead near western New South Wales Islamuddin Sajid 08 August 2026 • Update : 08 August 2026 ISLAMABAD Australia’s New South Wales government has confirmed two new cases of H5 avian influenza in native birds, bringing the state’s total to four, ABC News reported Saturday, citing an official government statement. The latest cases involved greater crested terns found dead near Narooma on the south coast and Wentworth in western New South Wales. The birds were reported by members of the public and tested by the state’s H5 response team. The first two New South Wales cases were detected in migratory petrels near Port Stephens in July. Environment Minister Penny Sharpe said the detections were not unexpected and the government was prepared to manage further impacts. Authorities are continuing surveillance in affected areas, while the government works with the poultry industry to strengthen biosecurity. No H5 cases have been detected in New South Wales poultry so far. Australian Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson said Friday that testing had confirmed another 20 positive detections in Victoria state, all involving greater crested terns in the Portland and Nelson area. Australia has now recorded 175 confirmed or presumed positive H5 bird flu detections based on tested samples. However, authorities said there had been no detections in poultry or Australia’s agricultural production system, while the risk to humans remained very low. Concerns have also prompted the Royal Adelaide Show to cancel bird and poultry exhibits scheduled for next month. Photo: File When highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza spread into U.S. dairy cattle, it raised the pressing question for farmers and regulators: what happens when virus‐contaminated dairy manure is spread on fields? That’s the focus of new research led by Dr. Tucker Burch of the USDA Agricultural Research Service. Why It Matters Poultry farms have tested positive shortly after nearby dairies spread manure. Nobody has proven a link, and proving one requires knowing whether viruses actually travel in the aerosol when a tanker is running. Why the lagoon became the question Burch spoke at an international conference about avian influenza, held in partnership with the University of Guelph. He outlined how viral and fecal bioaerosols are spread during dairy manure application. “The background here is the spillover of H5N1 into U.S. dairy cattle. This is a very novel challenge for the dairy industry. The virus was shed during this outbreak at very high titer in the milk. A lot of that actually ends up in the manure lagoons,” said Burch. In a study by Emory University, the avian influenza virus was found at multiple California dairy farms in several locations, including manure lagoons. That raised questions about manure management. Read Also Dairy Cattle The milk never leaves the farm, but it still moves through quota “Because it’s in the lagoon, there were lots of questions that came up,” said Burch. “What do we do with this waste? It needs to get land applied. Do we need to hold onto it for a certain amount of time (or) can it get applied right away? And then, during application, are there any concerns with aerosols drifting away from the application site?” There was added urgency to these questions after anecdotal reports of poultry farms that tested positive shortly after nearby dairy farms had spread manure. That suggested aerosols could be involved, even if the link hadn’t been proven. A decade of practice at catching things in the air Burch works in a joint USDA–USGS laboratory in central Wisconsin that operates closely with the University of Wisconsin Marshfield Agricultural Research Station, which has a dairy farm that milks about 120 cows and raises 400 to 500 heifers. He describes the farm as an ideal research partner. The research team has relevant experience. Nearly a decade ago, when Wisconsin dairies explored irrigation-based manure spreading using centre pivots and traveling guns, nearby residents worried those systems might spray zoonotic pathogens into the air. Burch’s group sampled the air for micro-organisms to assess risk. “If you’re collecting air samples to look at micro-organisms, there’s essentially three types of technology. You can impact the organisms on a solid media, you can impinge them in a liquid media, or you can filter them out,” he said. The process involved cumbersome gear including pumps, generators and extension cords. “To collect air samples for one hour, we usually spent two hours just moving equipment around.” In early 2024, as the dairy H5N1 outbreak unfolded, Burch encountered a battery‐operated air sampler made by NovaPrep (the cub sampler) that runs at very high flow rates, which means high concentration of material on a filter. What turned up inside the barns His team obtained several units and quickly put them to work at the research farm. Samples were taken in the milking parlour, dairy barn, heifer barn and transition barn for new arrivals, as well as at outdoor locations. Burch said he quickly learned how easily outdoor controls can be contaminated if placed too close to barns. Samples were analyzed for a suite of indigenous enteric viruses and for ruminant bacteroides, a bacterial marker in cattle feces. Patterns matched animal age groups. “We detected a variety of viruses on the farm and found some interesting and sensible correlations with probably the age of the livestock we were sampling,” said Burch. Bovine polyomavirus was found more often in the milking parlor, and both adenovirus and enterovirus were associated with younger animals. He said ruminant bacteroides appeared in every indoor air sample, although concentrations varied. Six metres from the tanker U.S. Department of Agriculture researchers are looking into what happens when virus‐contaminated dairy manure is spread on fields. The ongoing study is motivated from a 2024 outbreak of H5N1 avian influenza detected in U.S. dairy cattle. Photo: File Burch’s team wanted to test air during tanker-based manure application, so it ran a trial in 2025 in an approximately 400‐metre field. Samplers were set as close as six metres from the spread area. Manure samples from the tankers showed high levels of ruminant bacteroides, bovine adenovirus, coronavirus and enterovirus. In the downwind air, only the bacterial marker (ruminant bacteroidetes) appeared. Making sure tests are correct Although tests are more sensitive than they were in the past, there is still concern about adequate virus detection. Naturally occurring viruses in manure are too sparse and variable to serve as reliable tracers so the team is adding high concentrations E. coli into the tankers and tracking them downwind. The team is now planning to use coliphage (a type of bacteriophage) as a spiked viral marker in manure tankers. By adding large quantities of coliphage (approximately 100 quadrillion plaque-forming units of coliphage), they hope to create a detectable signal in downwind air samples, allowing for more powerful assessment of viral aerosolization and transport. Sampling the lagoon itself During his presentation, Burch credited Dr. Joseph Heffron, also from the USDA, for this plan B approach. Heffron also spoke at the conference about sampling methods for surveillance of livestock viruses in a dairy manure lagoon, with a particular focus on avian influenza and other enteric viruses. Heffron’s study, also at a University of Wisconsin Marshfield agricultural research station, used a two-stage lagoon system where the primary five-million-litre lagoon overflows into a secondary four-million-litre lagoon. Sampling strategies included perimeter sampling, centre-of-lagoon sampling using specialized lake samplers, and large-volume filtered samples from the secondary lagoon. He said lagoons are not only a potential source of environmental contamination when manure is land-applied, but also serve as important monitoring points for assessing herd health. “This is really the motivation of coming to, and this is the question that I want to answer, is how do we get from something that is tens of millions of litres down to six microlitres of template that we put into our PCR (polymerase chain reaction),” he said. While the recent study remains ongoing, key data findings so far include: What the lagoon sampling shows so far Sample the interior, not the edge. Virus concentrations are consistently higher in the lagoon interior than at the perimeter, so perimeter sampling alone is not sufficient. Do not agitate first. Agitating the lagoon increases fecal bacteria signals but marginally reduces virus detection, so agitation is not helpful when the goal is finding viruses. Replicate at every step. Multiple locations, multiple samples and multiple extractions are all important for reliable detection. records.content: Friday 14 August, 2026 Archive বাংলা HOME News PM President Top News National Arts & Entertainment July Uprising Education News Health News Climate Change & Environment Science & Technology Weather Business International District Interview Sports Notun Kuri Sports Subscriber NOTICE All News News Flash PM urges US companies to invest confidently, build long-term businesses in Bangladesh PM’s India, Japan visits not finalised yet: Shama PM pledges support to expand mathematics Olympiad at grassroots BNP submits nomination paper for Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir in presidential election Mirza Fakhrul set to hold highest constitutional position from grassroots News BSS 11 Aug 2026, 18:50 Update : 11 Aug 2026, 19:15 BLRI vaccines for avian flu, Gumboro disease handed over for commercial production: Rashid Photo: PID DHAKA, Aug 11, 2026, (BSS) - Vaccines for avian influenza and Gumboro disease developed by the Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute (BLRI) have been formally handed over to the Department of Livestock Services (DLS) for commercial production and expansion at the farmers’ level, said Fisheries and Livestock Minister Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid. “The vaccines, developed through indigenous technology and research, would play an important role in controlling diseases in the country’s poultry sector, reducing production costs and decreasing dependence on imports,” he said. He made the remarks at a vaccine handover ceremony held today at the conference room of the ministry at the secretariat here. Senior officials of the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock, director general of the Department of Livestock Services and Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute, scientists and researchers, university teachers and veterinarians, industry entrepreneurs, representatives of farmers and representatives of vaccine-producing companies attended the programme. Director General of the Department of Livestock Services Md. Shahnewaz Khan and Director General of the Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute Dr. Shakila Faruk, among other officials, were also present. Rashid said today’s event was not merely a formal handover of vaccines, but an important step towards taking knowledge and innovations achieved in laboratories to farmers at the field level. BLRI scientists and researchers developed the two vaccines using indigenous technology through years of research, testing and trials despite various challenges, he added. He said an invention completed in a laboratory cannot deliver its full benefit unless it is brought into practical use for ordinary people. Therefore, he said, the priority now is to take research-based innovations to the stage of commercial production and ensure their use at the farmers’ level. The minister said the BLRI-developed vaccines for avian influenza and Gumboro disease had been handed over to the Department of Livestock Services for commercial production. This has opened a new window of opportunity for the country’s poultry sector, he said, adding that if the concerned institutions work in coordination, it will be possible to make the vaccines available to farmers within a short time. He congratulated all scientists, researchers, officials and employees of BLRI involved in developing the vaccines, as well as those concerned with the Department of Livestock Services. He particularly expressed gratitude to those who worked in laboratories for a long time and contributed to developing the vaccines through testing and trials using indigenous technology and materials. At the programme, the minister also highlighted various government initiatives aimed at supporting agriculture and farmers. The country’s economy will also improve with the development of agriculture, he said, adding that the government is working to advance the overall economy by strengthening farmers and agriculture. Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid said the farmers’ economy would become stronger if they received fair prices for their products. Improvement in the economic condition of farmers would have a positive impact on the national economy, he said. As Bangladesh is an agriculture-based country, he said, agriculture needs to be further strengthened as one of the major driving forces of the economy in the coming days. Referring to the financial difficulties faced by farmers, the minister said the government has taken initiatives to resolve the longstanding loan-related problems of small and marginal farmers. He said loans of up to Taka 10,000 taken by small and marginal farmers who had faced difficulties in repaying them had been waived. The minister said the banks concerned did not suffer losses due to the loan waiver, as the government paid the banks the amount on behalf of the farmers. As a result, the farmers’ debt burden was reduced while the lending banks also received their dues, he said. Referring to various agriculture-based government programmes, he said initiatives including Family Card, Farmer Card and canal excavation programmes had been undertaken. He said the drainage system had weakened as canal excavation activities had remained largely suspended for a long time. As a result, even slight excessive rainfall caused waterlogging and sudden flooding in various areas. The minister said the government has adopted a five-year plan to revive canals across the country. Under the plan, excavation of designated canals is being carried out every year. The Ministry of Agriculture and other relevant departments are working according to their respective responsibilities. He said around 90 percent of canal excavation work under the Ministry of Agriculture had already been completed this year. The government institutions assigned with responsibilities must not merely show progress on paper, but prove progress through actual work, he added. Highlighting the importance of the Farmer Card in ensuring production and fair prices for farmers, the minister said the card would play an important role in providing farmers with advance information on which products would bring them greater profits at a particular time, which products are in demand in the market and what kind of assistance is required for production. Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid said farmers would also be provided with more effective support, from supplying necessary production inputs, including fertiliser and seeds, to ensuring fair prices for their products. He said if accurate information is delivered to farmers at the right time, production planning would become more effective and the risk of unnecessary supply shortages or overproduction in the market could be reduced. The minister also said registration for the Farmer Card was progressing rapidly. So far, registration of around 1.3 million farmers has been completed, he added. Although the government has a three-year plan for the programme, efforts are being made to complete the Farmer Card registration process ahead of the stipulated timeframe, he said. The minister said the livestock sector is also an important part of the country’s agricultural economy. If diseases in the poultry and livestock sectors are not controlled, farmers may face substantial financial losses, he said.
